>_**The main ablation shows that the coordinate representation collapses under DPO, but we do not see ablations that separately test: (i) a more structured prompt without Wyckoff; (ii) Wyckoff but no DPO; (iii) entropy regularization without temperature scheduling. So we cannot fully isolate what contributes most to the S.U.N. gain.**_

We agree that isolating these factors is important. Ablations (ii) and (iii) are already in Table 1: **PLaID++ (Non-DPO Types) Wyckoff** (which uses Wyckoff but no DPO) achieves 3.58% S.U.N., and **PLaID++ (DPO Types) Stability + Novelty** (which uses entropy regularization with constant temperature) reaches 6.22% S.U.N. These results show that both Wyckoff representation and temperature scheduling independently contribute to the overall S.U.N. gain. We have copied the corresponding rows below for convenience:

| Method                                      | Params   | Structural Validity (%) | Composition Validity (%) | Stability (%) | S.U.N. (%) |
|---------------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------|----------------------------|----------------|------------|
| PLaID++ (Non-DPO Types) — Wyckoff           | Wyckoff  | 99.80                     | 91.22                      | 7.17           | 3.58       |
| PLaID++ (DPO Types) — Stability + Novelty   | Stability + Novelty | 99.78 | 95.64 | 16.72 | 6.22 |
| PLaID++                                     | --       | 99.75                     | **97.34**                  | **22.27**      | **7.74**   |

We are not sure what the reviewer is referencing when they state “structured-but-non-Wyckoff”, but note that only the 3d-coordinate representation collapses under DPO, while Wyckoff+DPO remains stable, highlighting the unique benefit of the Wyckoff encoding. With additional context, we can perform specifically requested experiments. For further work regarding prompts, please refer to the rebuttal for Reviewer 13wd, where we experimented with prompt robustness.

>_**Are all preference pairs derived purely from model-generated samples, or do you also form pairs that include real MP-20 structures as positives? If yes, what is the ratio of synthetic–synthetic vs. real–synthetic pairs per iteration?**_

The PLaID++ pipeline only constructs preference pairs derived from model-generated samples such that our RL training is fully on-policy.

>_**You use eqV2 for training and eSEN for evaluation to mitigate reward hacking. Have you tried a third MLIP/evaluator (even a weaker one) to test whether the performance gains generalize across potentials, or do you observe overfitting to the two chosen models?**_

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern for potential overfitting of PLaID++ to eqV2 and eSEN. We evaluate PLaID++ generated crystals on the Orb-V3 conf-inf-mpa MLIP introduced in [1], obtaining a 25.2% stability rate and 8.3% S.U.N. rate, higher than the 22.27% stability and 7.74% S.U.N. rate evaluated on eSEN that was reported in the paper. These results reinforce our DFT results and indicate that our model is not specifically hacking to one MLIP or MLIP family.

[1] Orb-v3: atomistic simulation at scale. Rhodes et al. arXiv 2025

>_**Please provide the exact per-iteration temperature schedule. Also, can you compare “iterative DPO + temperature schedule” against “iterative SFT (no DPO) + the same temperature schedule”? This would clarify whether the diversity preservation comes from DPO or simply from sampling at higher T.**_

Regarding the temperature schedule, our exact per-iteration values are present in Figure 3 of the paper (0.7, 0.7, 0.9, 0.9, 1.1, 1.1, 1.3), and we have updated the font size of this figure in the main text to increase its readability. We increase temperature every other iteration to separate two learning dynamics: (1) at a fixed temperature, the model absorbs the preference signal and shifts toward more stable structures; (2) after this consolidation, a temperature increase broadens exploration, counteracting mode collapse and enabling new regions of chemical space to be surfaced for the next round of preference construction. Empirically, this schedule produced the best balance between stability improvements and S.U.N. preservation. We will include these pipeline details in the camera-ready to ensure full reproducibility. 

Thank you for bringing up the “iterative SFT (no DPO) + same temperature schedule” ablation! We are currently running this experiment and will report back soon.

## New Conditional Generation Results

In response to Reviewers W4wS and y1qQ’s suggestions, we have run new experiments to confirm that PLaID++ naturally extends to multi-objective, property-guided design by introducing a new property to our RLIP objective. We evaluate our model’s ability to generate crystals with a bulk modulus greater than 300 GPa, as these structures are promising candidates for superhard materials. Specifically, **we show that this PLaID++ variant achieves a new state of the art in unconditional generation (8.15%) and generates 60% more crystals satisfying a bulk modulus target of >300 GPa compared to SFT alone.**

We introduce the additional (accept, reject) preference pairs consisting of (stable & high bulk modulus, stable & low bulk modulus), (stable + novel & high bulk modulus, stable + novel & low bulk modulus), (stable & high bulk modulus, unstable & high bulk modulus) crystals. Note that we define “high bulk modulus” crystals as having a bulk modulus between 325 and 725 GPa as predicted by our eSEN MLIP. We restrict the range to [325, 725] to avoid outlier crystals in our dataset, which may reflect reward hacking to our MLIP rather than valid bulk modulus predictions. Previous work [1] has shown that MLIPs align with ground-truth DFT calculated bulk modulus values, giving us confidence that our model is generating crystals with realistic and useful properties.

We ablate our iterative DPO pipeline for bulk modulus trained jointly with the existing space group and stable/unstable crystal paper preference dataset (PLaID++ Joint Bulk Modulus) against the variant trained only on bulk modulus preference pairs (PLaID++ Bulk Modulus Only). Notably, the joint RLIP setting consistently outperforms the bulk-modulus-only pipeline, reinforcing that joint training helps rather than hurts property targeting, even when optimizing for a new objective. These results confirm that PLaID++ naturally extends to multi-objective, property-guided design, strengthening our claim that RLIP supports broad targeted generation beyond symmetry constraints.

|PLaID++ Variant                 | # High Bulk Modulus & SUN | # High Bulk Modulus |
|--------------------------------------|------------:|----------------:|
| Wyckoff Base (Non-DPO) | 25     | 38         |
| PLaID++ (Bulk Modulus Only)                     | 28      | 32       |
| **PLaID++ (Joint Bulk Modulus)**                 | **40**      | **54**          |


Additionally, we evaluate PLaID++ (Joint Bulk Modulus) on unconditional generation. Importantly, introducing bulk-modulus preferences alongside our existing stability, novelty, and space-group objectives further strengthens a central finding of our work: joint preference optimization across multiple tasks enhances unconditional materials generation. While generating superhard materials is an especially challenging objective—publicly available DFT data include only ~10k structures and fewer than 100 with bulk modulus >300 GPa—PLaID++ still generates 40% more crystals above this threshold. This indicates generalizability and the model’s ability to hillclimb in data-sparse regimes.


| PLaID++ Variant                  | S.U.N. % |
|--------------------------------------------------------|-------:|
| PLaID++ (Old)        | 7.74 |
| **PLaID++ (Joint Bulk Modulus)**     | **8.15** |

[1] Benchmarking Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Elastic Property Prediction. Gao et al. arXiv 2025


## PLaID++ Independent Validation

We also note that the recently released LeMat-GenBench benchmark [2] provides a standardized evaluation of generative crystal models, which independently corroborates PLaID++’s state-of-the-art results across S.U.N. and Stability metrics. Specifically, Table 12 in the LeMat-GenBench paper highlights that when using an MLIP ensemble (including MACE-MPA-0, UMA, and Orb V3) with MP-20 as the reference set, PLaID++ produces S.U.N. crystals at over 2x the rate of the next best model:

| **Model** | **E_hull (Std)** | **Stability %** | **S.U.N. %**   |
|--------------|------------------|-----------------|----------------|
| Crystal-GFN  | 1.66 ± 2.51 | 5.6 (141)  | 5.6 (141)  |
| DiffCSP++ | 0.39 ± 0.44  | 4.8 (121) | 3.4 (85)  |
| SymmCD  | 0.85 ± 1.07  | 4.3 (108)  | 2.2 (54)   |
| ADiT  | 0.32 ± 0.45 | 1.0 (25)  | 0.6 (15) |
| WyFormer-DFT | 0.24 ± 0.38  | 8.2 (205) | 4.0 (100) |
| MatterGen    | 0.16 ± 0.18  | 6.0 (150)  | 3.6 (91) |
| **PLaID++**      | **0.06 ± 0.17**  | **31.0 (776)**  | **11.6 (289)** |

Further, LeMat-GenBench finds that when evaluating using LeMat-Bulk as a reference set, which has 120x more crystal structures than MP-20, PLaID++ still produces S.U.N. crystals at over 2x the rate of the next best model. This result highlights that our novelty incentive in our RLIP pipeline generalizes to datasets beyond MP-20.

[2] LeMat-GenBench: A Unified Evaluation Pipeline for Crystal Generative Models. Duval et al., arXiv 2025.

>_**It is mentioned that the exploration "expands into areas underrepresented in the base model" and shows increased generation of P-block elements. Have you validated whether this represents valid exploration or bias? Have you compared generation patterns between the base pre-trained Qwen before SFT and PLaID++ to determine if the P-block favoritism comes from pre-training bias, SFT, or DPO learning?**_

The shift towards P-block elements does not come from pre-training: the base Qwen model (before any SFT) cannot generate syntactically valid crystal structures, so it has no meaningful compositional distribution to compare against. The shift only appears when comparing the Wyckoff SFT model and the final PLaID++ model, which isolates the effect to our reinforcement learning pipeline. Since DPO directly rewards stability and novelty, the incentive structure of our reward pushes the model to explore regions of chemical space like those of P-block metalloids, which are likely to be stable, yet are underrepresented in MP-20.

>_**Your conditional experiments focus on 7 space groups. Great point! We plan to run more property-guided experiments to demonstrate that PLaID++’s flexibility enables it to excel at other, non-space-group property-generation tasks. >_**For the 1k DFT relaxations, were the candidates sampled only from the final aligned model, or proportionally from all DPO iterations? If only from the last one, could this selection bias exaggerate the agreement between MLIP and DFT?**_

Thank you for the thoughtful question. Our 1k-sample DFT validation set was drawn from the final aligned PLaID++ model, rather than proportionally from all intermediate DPO iterations. We chose this design because the final checkpoint is the model intended for deployment and is therefore the distribution whose DFT agreement we ultimately care about. To address the MLIP-DFT discrepancy concern, we are currently expanding our DFT evaluation to a full 10k-sample relaxation, which will include crystals sampled across a wider diversity of prompts and conditions.

We thank the reviewers for their feedback. We begin with a general comment, and reply to each reviewer individually through separate posts.

Although the domains in which post-training has been applied are rapidly expanding, it is not obvious that RL would generalize well for generating *novel* inorganic crystal structures. This is because generating novel structures is inherently an out-of-distribution task, which RL generally struggles with.

Importantly, we show that a structured Wyckoff representation is not merely a different crystal formatting. Rather, we see that the coordinate-only representation’s S.U.N. rate collapses across DPO iterations despite higher stability rates; it is only with innovation at the representation level that we see generalization rather than memorization under preference optimization.

Additionally, our aim is not architectural novelty for its own sake; instead, we focus on the components that actually amplify high-throughput crystal discovery. First, our results directly speak to the bitter lesson, the idea that data scaling regimes outperform hand-crafted, bespoke models. In crystal discovery, geometry-aware or equivariant architectures (e.g., Wyckoff-Transformer-style models that embed Wyckoff sites as learned tokens) exist, yet PLaID++ outperforms them on all metrics relevant to discovery. This shows that algorithmic novelty is not the primary bottleneck for materials discovery; the core challenge is how to represent crystals and align models with physics-derived objectives.

Third, our preference-alignment framework demonstrates generalizability across data-sparse crystallographic objectives. As the field shifts towards conditional generation, a key challenge is that conditional generation tasks have orders of magnitude less data than unconditional S.U.N. crystal discovery. We chose space group conditioning as an exemplary conditional generation task since 224/230 space groups have <1,000 samples in our training data. We find that for materials discovery, there exists strong transferability between unconditional and conditional generation, with PLaID++ achieving SOTA results in both settings. Additionally, in response to Reviewer 13wd’s comments, we tested PLaID++’s space-group conditioned generation capabilities for 8 space groups not directly in our RL pipeline, and saw an average 20% improvement in S.S.U.N. rates. 

Reviewer 13wd notes that “what matters most is actual high-throughput discovery, not a pretty number.” We agree. Our methods yield a practical generator that produces 50% more stable, unique, novel crystals than prior work while being 5x faster than competing methods. In a field where equivariance and invariant compute-heavy architectures are notoriously slow and finicky (Joshi et al., 2025), demonstrating that outperforming specialized models with simple representations and principled alignment is a meaningful scientific contribution.

>_**The reward of preferences is narrow and model-based. All large-scale preference pairs come from MLIPs (eqV2 for training, eSEN for evaluation). Even though they separate train-time and eval-time models to reduce reward hacking, the model may still be aligned to this family of potentials rather than to actual DFT or experimental reality. The 1k DFT sanity check helps, but is too small to fully validate the main claim.**_

We agree that reliance on MLIP-derived preference pairs raises the question of whether PLaID++ might align to a family of interatomic potentials rather than true DFT or experimental behavior. As Reviewer 13wd noted, to directly assess this, we performed an MLIP–DFT correlation study on a diverse set of generated structures and found that eSEN predictions achieve $R^2 = 0.84$ when regressed against fully relaxed DFT energies. This strong correlation indicates that modern MLIPs provide a sufficiently accurate and smooth approximation of DFT energetics for constructing preference signals, and as MLIP quality continues to improve, the gap between proxy rewards and ground truth will narrow further.

We fully acknowledge that a 1k-sample DFT validation is only an initial step. To address this concern, we are currently running a full 10,000-structure DFT relaxation campaign for the final version of the paper. This will provide a full, model-independent benchmark of stability, novelty, and S.U.N. characteristics beyond MLIP families. 

Additionally, to address the reviewer’s concerns for potential overfitting to eqV2 and eSEN, **we evaluate PLaID++ generated crystals on Orb-V3 conf-inf-mpa MLIP,** introduced in [1], obtaining a 25.2% stability rate and 8.3% S.U.N. rate, higher than the 22.27% stability and 7.74% S.U.N. rate evaluated on eSEN that was reported in the paper.

[1] Orb-v3: atomistic simulation at scale. Rhodes et al. arXiv 2025

>_**Can you report transfer? For example, train on MP-20 but prompt for a space group that is rare in MP-20, or generate crystals with >20 atoms, or test on a different dataset split. Right now it’s unclear how generalizable the method is beyond MP-20.**_

Great question! Please refer to **Figures 9 and 10** in the Appendix of our updated paper for a direct comparison of the S.S.U.N. rate and percent correct space group between PLaID Wyckoff Base and PLaID++ (with RLIP). We sampled PLaID++ on 8 new space groups excluded from the set of space groups we directly optimized for in our RLIP pipeline. For these new space groups we see a 20% improvement on SSUN compared to fine-tuning alone, demonstrating that **reinforcement learning provides benefit to tasks that are not explicitly incentivized by our reward structure**. This applies even for rare space groups in MP-20. For example space group $P2_13$ with only 67 occurrences in the training set sees a 26% improvement in SSUN. Notably, Figure 10 demonstrates that the improvements come from more than simply generating more stable materials—the proportion of materials that correctly satisfy the space group constraint also increases for many of the space groups. This highlights the benefits of a unified foundational model across many tasks, and suggests our RL approach learns generalizable structural principles that apply across space groups rather than merely memorizing training distribution patterns.

We also see that PLaID++ generalizes to materials with larger unit cells than in the training distribution, as 5.66% of the crystals generated by our PLaID++ model have > 20 atoms. On the other hand, the PLaID++ ablation with the 3D-coordinate-based representation only has 0.08% of crystals with > 20 atoms. This demonstrates how our information-dense, Wyckoff-based representation allows the model to generalize from small unit cell sizes.

>_**No new neural architecture; novelty is mostly procedural.**_

Thanks for the question. We address novelty in the top-level comment addressed to all reviewers.

>_**All training/evaluation is on MP-20 only. The model never leaves this relatively standard ~45k-material dataset with ≤20 atoms. There is no demonstration on larger or more diverse datasets (Alexandria, LeMat-Bulk, etc.) and no zero-shot transfer experiment. So we don’t know if PLaID++ is general, or just very tuned to MP-20 chemistry space.**_

Thank you for raising this important point. We follow the prevailing standard in the crystal‐generation literature by conducting all training and evaluation on MP-20. Nearly all recent generative materials papers—CDVAE, DiffCSP, FlowMM, FlowLLM, CrystalLLM, and ADiT—evaluate solely on MP-20, making it the only fully established benchmark that allows meaningful, apples-to-apples comparison. To ensure fair and reproducible comparison against prior work, we adopt the same protocol.

>_**Prompt robustness is not explored. The model is always prompted with essentially the same English template (“Below is a description of a bulk material… The spacegroup number is X… Generate…”).**_

We disagree with the premise that prompt-wording robustness is central to our setting. PLaID++ is not primarily designed to be a chatbot-style natural language interface. Rather, we leverage an LLM backbone such that training and sampling for many different generation tasks can be unified under one language-based framework. All objectives (unconditional generation, space-group control, downstream property targeting, etc…) flow through the same text interface, meaning that we can combine tasks, mix conditioning information, and extend to new scientific objectives without changing the architecture. This is the core flexibility we claim.

That said, we acknowledge that our current model overfits to a single prompt template: we used one phrasing during SFT and DPO, and the alignment loop naturally reinforces it. If prompt-paraphrase robustness is desired, we can straightforwardly incorporate multiple phrasings into the DPO dataset. The limitation is in the specific setup we chose, not in the method itself. Our methodology focuses on highlighting the strength of the unified generation setup, and to further support it, as requested by the reviewer, we will retrain PLaID++ to target crystals with specific properties.

summary.value: The paper presents PLaID++ which is a language model-based approach for generating stable inorganic crystal structures by combining a Wyckoff position-based text representation with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) training. The work uses Reinforcement Learning from Interatomic Potentials (RLIP). The model uses the eqV2 MMLIP for structure relaxation and evaluation. Then they use a tiered preference pairing system to create preference pairs for DPO optimization. The authors report sota performance on the MP-20 benchmark with a 22.27% stability rate and a 7.74% S.U.N. rate.

strengths.value:
1. Multiple MLIPs are employed for rigorous validation. They use separate MLIPs for training (eqV2) and evaluation (eSEN) prevents reward hacking, and the inclusion of DFT validation on a 1000-sample subset provides ground-truth verification. 

2. The dual strategy for diversity is an innovative practice. The combination of a symmetry-aware representation with Wyckoff positions and dynamic temperature scheduling during DPO training is innovative for encouraging diversity and preventing potential mode collapse. 

3. The reported sampling speed shows advantage over diffusion-based methods.

weaknesses.value:
1. The tiered preference pairing scheme is a key contribution of the work and crucial design choice. The design are claimed valid but. rather intuitive and lacks rationale. The work would benefit from a thorough ablation study for e.g. the tiering threshold, pairing strategy, sample portions, etc.

2. The dynamic temperature schedule is described as critical for maintaining diversity. But the work lacks the analysis of sensitivity to temperature e.g. tracking how temperature changes affect exploration patterns or causally lead to the design of S.U.N. materials. The research gap remains to understand the improvements reported in the paper.

questions.value:
1. How was the metastable threshold (0.08 eV/atom) determined? Why you choose the specific tiered preference pairing scheme? Have you performed ablation experiments, e.g. use only the (metastable, unstable) pairs, considering the often noised predictions for the 'stable' crystal structures with MLIPs? In addition, how does the sampling ratio contributes to the final performance gain?
2. How sensitive is the final S.U.N. rate to the hyperparameters of the temperature schedule? 
3. I believe some samples would fail the relaxation, are they regarded as unstable or disgarded?
4. It is mentioned that the exploration "expands into areas underrepresented in the base model" and shows increased generation of P-block elements. Have you validated whether this represents valid exploration or bias? Have you compared generation patterns between the base pre-trained Qwen before SFT and PLaID++ to determine if the P-block favoritism comes from pre-training bias, SFT, or DPO learning?

summary.value:
This paper presents PLaID++, a preference-aligned large language model for inorganic crystal generation. The model fine-tunes a pretrained Qwen-2.5 7B LLM using a new Wyckoff-based textual representation that encodes symmetry and lattice parameters compactly, then post-trains it via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

The authors adapt DPO into a scientific alignment framework called RLIP (Reinforcement Learning from Interatomic Potentials): generated crystals are evaluated with machine-learning interatomic potentials (eqV2, eSEN) for stability, novelty, and space-group correctness, and ranked into preference pairs (e.g., stable > metastable > unstable). Iterative DPO updates align the model toward physically stable and diverse structures, while a dynamic-temperature schedule prevents mode collapse.

On the MP-20 dataset, PLaID++ achieves 97.3 % stability and a 7.7 % S.U.N. (Stable-Unique-Novel) rate, roughly 50 % higher than prior methods such as FlowLLM and ADiT. Joint training on unconditional and space-group-conditioned prompts also improves targeted generation (↑ 47 % S.S.U.N.). Ablations show that the Wyckoff representation, tiered stability rewards, and dynamic temperature are key to these gains.

strengths.value:
- Clear problem framing and relevance. The paper targets a high-impact task: generating novel, thermodynamically stable inorganic crystals, potentially conditioned on structural symmetry. This is central to materials discovery and of broad scientific interest.

- They check their reward model.
They do attempt to show that MLIP-based energy ranking is not totally hallucinated. They correlate MLIP-based energy above hull with true DFT energy above hull on 1,000 samples, and report R² ~0.84 for eSEN near the stability threshold. They also report classification precision/recall for “stable vs metastable vs unstable,” which matters because the entire RLIP pipeline depends on the surrogate reward being aligned with physics.

- Computational throughput / practicality.
They emphasize that PLaID++ can sample 10,000 crystals in ~23 minutes on a single H100 and achieves ~5× higher throughput than FlowLLM. High-throughput suggests this may actually be usable for screening, not just a pretty table.

weaknesses.value:
- No new neural architecture; novelty is mostly procedural.
The backbone is Qwen-2.5 7B with LoRA. There is no new model class, no new attention mechanism, no new equivariant layer, no new geometry-aware transformer. The “innovation” is:
- - a structured text format (Wyckoff),
- - a preference-alignment / DPO loop using physics-derived rewards,
- - and some engineering heuristics (tiered rewards, temperature ramp).
This is valuable, but reviewers will ask: is this ICLR-level novelty, or is it an application of known LLM post-training techniques to a new domain?

- All training/evaluation is on MP-20 only.
The model never leaves this relatively standard ~45k-material dataset with ≤20 atoms. There is no demonstration on larger or more diverse datasets (Alexandria, LeMat-Bulk, etc.) and no zero-shot transfer experiment. So we don’t know if PLaID++ is general, or just very tuned to MP-20 chemistry space.


- Prompt robustness is not explored.
The model is always prompted with essentially the same English template (“Below is a description of a bulk material… The spacegroup number is X… Generate…”). There is no ablation on prompt phrasing, no test of whether the generation is brittle to different wording, no demonstration of controllability beyond “give me space group N.”
For a claimed “LLM interface,” this is under-explored. We don’t learn how instruction-like this really is vs how template-locked it is.

- No multi-objective targeting beyond symmetry.
They only condition on space group (as a proxy for symmetry class). They mention other properties (band gap, etc.) in the prompt template during SFT, but the reported experiments don’t actually demonstrate controllable generation for properties like band gap or conductivity. For discovery workflows, that’s critical. Right now, controllability is still narrow.



- Figures could be more readable.
Several figures (e.g., Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 8) have very small font on axes and legends. For a paper that leans heavily on ablation plots to support its claims (temperature schedule, S.U.N. over iterations, MLIP-vs-DFT correlation), readability matters. Increasing font size / contrast in these plots would make the empirical story much easier to audit.

questions.value:
- How sensitive is performance to the exact wording / structure of the prompt template? Can the model handle natural variations in phrasing, or is it essentially bound to the provided template?

- You frame PLaID++ as “preference aligned” via RLIP. In normal RLHF, preferences come from humans and implicitly encode high-level goals. Here, preferences come from MLIPs and symmetry filters. Do you observe any reward hacking behavior (i.e., crystals that look unphysical to a human crystallographer but score as “stable” under eqV2/eSEN)?

- Can you report transfer? For example, train on MP-20 but prompt for a space group that is rare in MP-20, or generate crystals with >20 atoms, or test on a different dataset split. Right now it’s unclear how generalizable the method is beyond MP-20.

- The font size / legend readability in key figures (3, 4) is quite small. Please enlarge axis labels and legends so that stability / S.U.N. trends and correlation plots can be evaluated without zooming.

summary.value: This paper proposes PLaID++, a preference-aligned LLM framework for inorganic crystal structure generation. PLalD++ first cast the crystal design into a text generation problem using a symmetry-aware Wyckoff-based representation, trained on MP-20 with SFT on top of Qwen2.5-7B. Then it introduces RLIP (Reinforcement Learning from Interatomic Potentials): the model samples candidate crystals, an ML interatomic potential assigns stability-related scores (stable/metastable/unstable), these scores are converted into preference pairs, and the model is iteratively updated with DPO. A key engineering choice is a temperature-increasing sampling schedule during iterative DPO to prevent diversity collapse.

strengths.value:
1. Treating crystal design as conditional/unconditional text generation and then doing preference-based post-training is a clean and extensible design that the broader LLM-for-science community can reuse.

2. Using ML interatomic potentials to create automatic preference pairs and feeding them to DPO is a nice instantiation of “RLHF without humans” for material science domains. It avoids training a separate value model and keeps the pipeline relatively simple.

3. The paper gives evidence that doing iterative preference optimization on a naive coordinate representation leads to mode/dictionary collapse, while the Wyckoff-based representation maintains S.U.N. This is a useful empirical observation for future work on structure-generators.

weaknesses.value:
1. The reward of preferences is narrow and model-based. All large-scale preference pairs come from MLIPs (eqV2 for training, eSEN for evaluation). Even though they separate train-time and eval-time models to reduce reward hacking, the model may still be aligned to this family of potentials rather than to actual DFT or experimental reality. The 1k DFT sanity check helps, but is too small to fully validate the main claim.


2. Targeted design is only partially demonstrated. The title says “targeted inorganic materials design,” but the actual conditional task is mainly space-group conditioning on 7 groups. That is narrower than what “targeted” typically implies in materials (e.g., band gap, stability window, mechanical property). The method may extend, but the paper does not show it.


3. Some pipeline details are underspecified. For iterative DPO, the paper does not clearly tabulate per-iteration: number of samples, number of preference pairs, positive/negative distribution across space groups, and exact temperature schedule. That makes it harder to reproduce and to judge whether the gains come from DPO itself or just from resampling at a higher temperature.


4. The main ablation shows that the coordinate representation collapses under DPO, but we do not see ablations that separately test: (i) a more structured prompt without Wyckoff; (ii) Wyckoff but no DPO; (iii) entropy regularization without temperature scheduling. So we cannot fully isolate what contributes most to the S.U.N. gain.


5. Given that this is a design paper, an example of “top-N generated structures sent for expert or database validation” would have made the story more convincing.

questions.value:
1. Are all preference pairs derived purely from model-generated samples, or do you also form pairs that include real MP-20 structures as positives? If yes, what is the ratio of synthetic–synthetic vs. real–synthetic pairs per iteration?


2. You use eqV2 for training and eSEN for evaluation to mitigate reward hacking. Have you tried a third MLIP/evaluator (even a weaker one) to test whether the performance gains generalize across potentials, or do you observe overfitting to the two chosen models?

3. Please provide the exact per-iteration temperature schedule. Also, can you compare “iterative DPO + temperature schedule” against “iterative SFT (no DPO) + the same temperature schedule”? This would clarify whether the diversity preservation comes from DPO or simply from sampling at higher T.


4. Your conditional experiments focus on 7 space groups. How would the pipeline change if the target were an observable (e.g., band gap > 2 eV, or formation energy below some threshold) instead of a space group? Can MLIP scores be turned into preferences for such targets without retooling the whole pipeline?


5. For the 1k DFT relaxations, were the candidates sampled only from the final aligned model, or proportionally from all DPO iterations? If only from the last one, could this selection bias exaggerate the agreement between MLIP and DFT?

comment.value:
> _**How was the metastable threshold (0.08 eV/atom) determined? Why do you choose the specific tiered preference pairing scheme? Have you performed ablation experiments, e.g. use only the (metastable, unstable) pairs, considering the often noised predictions for the 'stable' crystal structures with MLIPs? In addition, how does the sampling ratio contribute to the final performance gain?**_

Crystal-generation literature in CrystalLLM (Gruver et al., 2024), FlowMM (Miller et al., 2024), and prior MP-20–based works is split between using $\leq 0.08$ eV/atom and $\leq 0.1$ eV/atom as the metastability threshold. These papers use the $\leq 0.08$ eV/atom and $\leq 0.1$ eV/atom window to identify DFT-reachable metastable structures, reflecting both empirical synthesizability and the intrinsic uncertainty floor of MLIP predictions.

We choose to use the $\leq 0.1$ eV/atom threshold for evaluation since it has become more standard in the past year, allowing for equal comparison against other models. However, we choose the $\leq 0.08$ eV/atom threshold when constructing preference pairs since this threshold is more conservative and accounts for the noise present in MLIP predictions, reducing the likelihood of overfitting to one MLIP.

Our tiered preference pairing scheme and its 1:2 sampling ratio are chosen since smaller ratios perform worse as our training dataset becomes noticeably smaller, and larger ratios perform worse as the model overfits to each positive sample and consequently generates less diverse structures and lower S.U.N. rates.

We appreciate the suggestion to include more thorough design choice ablations. We are happy to add alternative thresholds and different sampling ratios to the camera-ready version should the reviewers consider it important, and we are currently running the ablation on only using (metastable, unstable) pairs in our tiering scheme, and will report our results as soon as they are available.

>_**The dynamic temperature schedule is described as critical for maintaining diversity. But the work lacks the analysis of sensitivity to temperature e.g. tracking how temperature changes affect exploration patterns or causally lead to the design of S.U.N. materials. How sensitive is the final S.U.N. rate to the hyperparameters of the temperature schedule?**_

We agree that temperature plays a key role in the exploration–exploitation tradeoff, and we did examine schedules that varied the temperature more frequently in the paper. At higher temperatures, the model has more trouble learning to generate stable structures, but can explore a greater breadth of chemical space. We tested increasing the temperature by 0.1 every iteration and 0.2 every iteration, and both led to the same failure mode: increasing temperature at each iteration pushes exploration faster than the model can adapt through DPO, preventing it from reliably improving stability between rounds. In these schedules, both models collapse early (Iteration 4), and S.U.N. performance drops below their previous iteration.

Hence, we use the more conservative schedule that increases temperature by 0.2 every two iterations in our flagship PLaID++ model. We increase the temperature every other iteration to separate two learning dynamics: (1) at a fixed temperature, the model absorbs the preference signal and shifts toward more stable structures; (2) after this consolidation, a temperature increase broadens exploration, counteracting mode collapse and enabling new regions of chemical space to be surfaced for the next round of preference construction. Empirically, this schedule produced the best balance between stability improvements and S.U.N. preservation. We will include these pipeline details in the camera-ready to ensure full reproducibility.

For now, **please refer to Figure 7** in the appendix of our updated paper for a plot of the S.U.N. performance of the different iterative temperature schemes.

>_**I believe some samples would fail the relaxation, are they regarded as unstable or are they discarded?**_

Samples that fail relaxation are treated as unstable, not discarded. Any non-convergent structure is assigned a high final energy, so it automatically fails the stability criterion. However, it remains in the evaluation set. In response to Reviewer y1qQ, we have included detailed DPO preference dataset information.
